final_message:
All three versions are done and pass every sample byte-exactly.

**Algorithm (shared)** — Jacobi stencil with two buffers. Walls/borders contribute the cell's own value, so I fold that in statically: each open cell gets `coef = 4 + (# wall/outside neighbours)` precomputed once, walls are stored as 0, and a step is just `(coef*old + up+down+left+right) >> 3` (values are non-negative and ≤ 9000, so `>>3` equals `//8` and everything fits in `i32`). Sources/walls are restored (or never written) each step. Sum/max/checksum are computed over open cells only, in row-major order for the tie-break.

**Speed choices per version**

- [rust/src/main.rs](/D:/projects/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder/heat/rust/src/main.rs) — padded flat `Vec<i32>` (zero border), plus a precomputed list of open-cell padded indices with their `u8` coefficients, so the inner loop is branch-free with unchecked indexing over only open cells; manual byte-level header parsing; LTO + `codegen-units=1` in [rust/Cargo.toml](/D:/projects/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder/heat/rust/Cargo.toml). Single thread.
- [plain.py](/D:/projects/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder/heat/plain.py) — the whole grid is packed into one Python `int`, 32 bits per cell. Shifts by one cell / one row give all four neighbours at once, precomputed bit-masks select neighbour-vs-own per cell, and the per-lane sum (≤ 72000) never carries across lanes; a mask after `>>3` clears cross-lane bits, and sources are OR-ed back. This replaces 40M Python-level cell updates with ~20 C-level bigint ops per step. Output via `sys.stdout.buffer` to keep `\n` line endings exact on Windows.
- [fast.py](/D:/projects/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder/heat/fast.py) — contiguous unpadded `int32` NumPy arrays (unpadded measured ~2× faster than padded views), all updates in-place with `out=`/`+=`/`>>=` to avoid temporaries, non-open cells restored by one flat fancy-index assignment per step; stats via `argmax` on open cells only (first max = row-major tie-break).

**Verification** — s1, s2, s3 pass byte-exact for rust, plain, and fast (9/9). I also checked all three against an independent brute-force Python reference on 60 random small grids (sizes 1–8, S ∈ {0,1,2,5,17,40}) plus a CRLF-input case: all matched. On a generated 400×400, S=250 benchmark all three outputs agreed; rough timings here were Rust ~0.11 s, fast.py ~0.9 s, plain.py ~1.3–2.3 s (machine was shared, so treat these as indicative).

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
